The sentence "Some firefighters rescue victims from danger" implies the existence of at least one firefighter. So, we start with an existential quantifier for firefighters: (∃x)Fx. For this firefighter, they rescue victims from danger. This means there must exist at least one victim (∃y)Vy and at least one danger (∃z)Dz. The predicate Rxyz means 'x rescues y from z', where x is the firefighter, y is the victim, and z is the danger. Combining these, we get: (∃x){Fx • (∃y)[Vy • (∃z)(Dz • Rxyz)]}. Let's evaluate the options:
A) (∃x){Fx • (∀y)[Dy ⊃ (∃z)(Vz • Rxyz)]} - This implies 'for all dangers', which is incorrect. It also swaps the roles of y and z in Rxyz.
B) (∃x){Fx • (∃y)[Vy • (∃z)(Dz • Rxyz)]} - This correctly translates to 'There exists a firefighter x such that x is a firefighter AND there exists a victim y such that y is a victim AND there exists a danger z such that z is a danger AND x rescues y from z'. This matches the original sentence.
C) (∃x){Fx • (∃y)(∃z)[(Vy • Dz) • Rxzy]} - This uses Rxzy, which would mean 'x rescues z from y'. According to the definition Rxyz: x rescues y from z, so y is the victim and z is the danger. Rxzy would mean z is the victim and y is the danger, which is incorrect.
